raw_response.country: United States (Alabama case narrative; broader global/Western democracies overview)

criterion_notes.c1: The essay topically discusses human rights and inequities in household and community water and sanitation access across Western democracies and the rural United States (citing secondary studies on incomplete plumbing, rural straight pipes, refugee camp latrines, and municipal water exclusion), although its main detailed subsection on Uniontown, Alabama (Section 6) shifts focus to municipal wastewater treatment plant (WWTP) effluent overflows into creeks rather than household service access.
criterion_notes.c2: Plain wording vs. narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading: Under the plain broad wording of Criterion 2, the paper discusses legal and regulatory factors—specifically the omission of water and sanitation rights from Western constitutions, UN human-rights resolutions, and environmental regulatory enforcement lapses (ADEM Notices of Violation, a 2008 consent decree, NPDES discharge permit renewals, and a stop-work order) at the Uniontown WWTP—so it satisfies the plain wording of Criterion 2 (though the overall study is still excluded under plain_criterion2_decision because it fails c3, c4, and c5). Under the active 2026-10-13 narrow rule-type mechanism reading, Criterion 2 is NOT met (c2 = no): constitutional political philosophy represents unanalysed macro-governance/normative background, and Clean Water Act NPDES effluent/overflow enforcement at a wastewater treatment lagoon regulates environmental surface-water pollution rather than a rule-type mechanism directly governing household or community service access (such as eligibility screening, administrative burden, documentation/tenure rules, tariffs, disconnection, or utility service-extension rules).
criterion_notes.c3: Published in a philosophy journal (Azafea: Revista de Filosofía), this article is a normative political-philosophy essay and narrative policy overview with no methods section, no systematic synthesis protocol, and no empirical study design. All figures on household water/sanitation access are secondary citations to prior literature and census tables, while the Uniontown WWTP narrative compiles publicly posted ADEM sanitary sewer overflow filings and mentions an unpublished creek E. coli observation without any reported empirical methodology (exclude as E05).
criterion_notes.c4: No primary or systematically synthesized empirical outcome measuring household or community access, connection, service availability, reliability, continuity, quantity, affordability, or exclusion is reported; household sanitation figures are secondary citations, and the Uniontown WWTP figures measure environmental sewage overflow volume (gallons discharged into Cottonwood and Freetown Creeks) and surface-water E. coli concentrations.
criterion_notes.c5: No empirical study design is reported or identifiable, and there is no empirical population/sample or exposure-outcome analysis linking a service-access rule or governance mechanism to a household or community access outcome.
criterion_notes.c6: Full text is in English (with English and Spanish abstracts) and is eligible without translation.

evidence_quotes.quote: The political philosophy that motivated the development of Western democracies emerges from an analysis of their foundational documents.

Despite the historical omission of rights to water and sanitation from the constitutions of most democracies, any government that fails to provide such access and protection is failing in its contract with its people.

Alabama, particularly the “Black Belt” of Alabama, provides a model for the nexus of race, economics, governmental competence or malfeasance, and regulatory failure in the provision of water and sanitation.

Although there was legal enforcement action by ADEM as early as 2005 (ADEM, 2005) followed by a binding legal action in which Uniontown agreed to fix its problems within 3 years (consent decree) in 2008 (ADEM, 2008a); in 2019 Uniontown is still waiting and the chronic overflows continue.

Uniontown is an exceptional model of systemic failure because both the lagoon and the spray field continue spilling contaminated water into two disparate creeks, and fouling two watersheds, for 11 years after a binding consent decree to eliminate sanitary sewer overflows within three years (ADEM, 2008a).

raw_response.outcome: not reported for service access (Uniontown WWTP narrative summarizes sanitary sewer overflow volumes in gallons and creek E. coli concentrations)
raw_response.population_and_sample: not reported (no empirical sample; narrative overview citing secondary data on Alabama Black Belt counties and public regulatory filings for Uniontown municipal WWTP)
raw_response.rationale: Excluded as E05 (No empirical evidence). This philosophy-journal article (Azafea: Revista de Filosofía) is a normative human-rights and political-philosophy essay combined with a narrative overview of water and sanitation issues and an unmethodological narrative account of chronic environmental sewage overflows at the Uniontown, Alabama municipal wastewater treatment plant (WWTP). It contains no empirical methods section, no identifiable empirical study design, and no primary or systematically synthesized empirical data on household or community water or sanitation service access (all household access statistics are secondary citations to prior studies). Furthermore, under the 2026-10-13 narrow Criterion 2 clarification, neither its broad constitutional philosophy discussion nor the Clean Water Act NPDES effluent/overflow enforcement actions at the Uniontown sewage lagoon constitute a rule-type mechanism directly governing household or community service access, and the Uniontown figures track environmental creek pollution (gallons of WWTP overflow) rather than a service-access outcome. Even under the plain broad wording of Criterion 2, the paper remains excluded (plain_criterion2_decision = exclude) for lack of empirical access evidence, identifiable study design, and empirical access outcomes.
raw_response.study_design: not reported (normative philosophical essay and narrative commentary without empirical methods)
